1	---
2	name: job-hunt
3	description: Find, verify and rank live job and contract openings that fit Prabhavit's CV — AI/automation engineering, forward-deployed and solutions engineering, full-stack product engineering, technical PM — remote-first from Italy but worldwide in scope, delivered as a ranked .xlsx shortlist. Use this skill whenever the conversation turns to looking for work: "find me some jobs", "any new roles this week", "who's hiring for X", "check openings at <company>", "any freelance or contract gigs going", "is this posting worth applying to", or a request to compare or re-rank roles already found. Trigger even when the request is vague ("anything interesting out there?"), names no job board, or mentions only a company or a technology rather than a role.
4	---
5	
6	# Job hunt
7	
8	Prabhavit is looking for work right now — his FlowSpace contract ended in July 2026. What
9	helps him is a short list of openings that are **real, currently open, and genuinely open to
10	him**, each with an honest reason it's worth an application. What hurts him is volume: a dead
11	link, a role that turns out to be US-payroll-only, or a staff-level posting he has no chance at
12	costs him more time than a missed opportunity does. Bias the whole process towards precision.
13	
14	Two references do the heavy lifting:
15	
16	- `references/candidate-profile.md` — what "good fit" means. **Read it before every sweep.** It holds his eligibility, target titles, seniority band, hard gates and preferences.
17	- `references/sources.md` — the tested search playbook: which domains and URL patterns actually return live postings, which are dead ends, and the specific ways postings lie. **Read it before your first search in a session.**
18	
19	Don't interview him before starting. He's already told the skill what he wants; ask at most one
20	question, and only when the answer would change the entire sweep (for example, if he names a
21	company that has no public board). Otherwise run the default sweep and note your assumptions in
22	the reply.
23	
24	## Step 1 — frame the sweep
25	
26	Set five parameters before searching. Anything the request specifies overrides these defaults:
27	
28	| Parameter | Default |
29	|---|---|
30	| Tracks | All four from the profile, weighted A (AI/automation) > B (forward-deployed/solutions) > C (full-stack/product) > D (technical PM) |
31	| Geography | Worldwide, prioritised by the eligibility tiers in the profile — mostly Tier 1, a minority of Tier 3 |
32	| Work basis | Employment **and** contract/freelance, in the same sheet, flagged so he can compare a day rate against a salary |
33	| Freshness | Posted within 30 days; prefer the last 7 |
34	| Size | 12–20 verified roles |
35	
36	A narrow request ("just contract work", "only n8n stuff", "anything at ElevenLabs") narrows the
37	sweep — don't pad it back out with unrelated roles to hit a count.
38	
39	## Step 2 — sweep wide before filtering
40	
41	Cast a much wider net than the final sheet, because most candidates die at verification. Aim for
42	**40+ raw candidates**; fewer than ~25 means the sweep was too narrow, and the fix is almost
43	always vocabulary — the same job is posted as "AI Automation Engineer", "Applied AI Engineer",
44	"Solutions Engineer" and "Automation Consultant" at four different companies.
45	
46	Run these in parallel in a single message (see `sources.md` for exact syntax and templates):
47	
48	1. Two or three `WebSearch` calls with `allowed_domains` on the ATS hosts — one per track.
49	2. One contract-vocabulary query using the literal words that work: `"contract"`, `"6-month contract"`, `freelance`, `B2B`, `part time`, `fractional`.
50	3. One stack-keyword query — `n8n`, `low-code`, `AI agents`, `Bubble.io`. These postings are much less crowded and are his sharpest edge.
51	4. Two or three board fetches — euremotejobs region paths, remoterocketship with `sort=DateAdded`, himalayas (serialize these, it rate-limits).
52	
53	If subagents are available, fan the sweep out: give each agent one source family and a fixed
54	return shape (title, company, url, location wording, comp, posted date, basis). Verification is
55	fetch-heavy, so parallelising the discovery leaves budget for it. Tell each agent to use only
56	WebSearch/WebFetch — curl and python fetching are prohibited in this environment.
57	
58	## Step 3 — filter against the profile
59	
60	Apply the hard gates from `candidate-profile.md` — language requirements he can't meet, deep ML
61	specialisation, agencies and aggregator reposts with no named end client, unpaid or
62	talent-pool listings. Being outside the EU is **not** a gate any more; it moves a role to
63	eligibility Tier 3 with a `Relocation` or `Sponsorship` flag.
64	
65	Keep a short list of notable drops and why. When the sheet comes back with 14 roles instead of
66	40, he should be able to see that the filter did the work rather than wondering whether the
67	search was lazy.
68	
69	## Step 4 — verify every survivor by fetching it
70	
71	He will click every link in the sheet, so every row must come from a page you actually loaded.
72	Never list a role from a search snippet alone, and never reconstruct a URL that looks plausible.
73	
74	For each candidate:
75	
76	- Normalise the URL first (strip Ashby's `?embed=js`, `/application`, `?utm_data=…`; add `?language=en` on Personio).
77	- Fetch it, and pull: exact title, company, the **eligibility sentence** (not the word "Remote" in the title), comp or rate if disclosed, posted date, seniority requirement, and whether it's employment or contract.
78	- **If a single-posting fetch comes back describing many different jobs, the posting is closed** — Greenhouse silently serves the board index for dead roles and nothing else signals it. Drop it.
79	- Drop anything you can't confirm is live. A quiet omission is better than a broken row.
80	- When a posting looks strong but the fetch is ambiguous, check the company's JSON board API (`sources.md` §5) rather than guessing.
81	
82	## Step 5 — score honestly
83	
84	```
85	Fit = role & track match        30
86	    + eligibility & work basis  25
87	    + stack overlap             20
88	    + seniority realism         15
89	    + signal quality            10
90	```
91	
92	- **Role & track match** — how close the actual responsibilities are to what he's done, not how good the title sounds.
93	- **Eligibility & work basis** — Tier 1 (workable from Italy today) scores full marks; Tier 2 (non-EU Europe, remote) most of them; Tier 3 (relocation or sponsorship) a fraction. A company willing to engage a contractor abroad scores as Tier 1 even if it's US-based.
94	- **Stack overlap** — named tools he has shipped with beat adjacent ones. `n8n` in a JD is worth more than a generic "Python required".
95	- **Seniority realism** — will they actually interview someone with ~3 years and no CS degree?
96	- **Signal quality** — freshness, disclosed comp, company type, clear scope.
97	
98	Use the range. If every role scores 82–88 the scores carry no information and he can't triage;
99	a real sweep produces a spread. Bands: **80+** apply this week · **65–79** solid, worth an
100	application · **50–64** worth a look if the top of the list dries up. Below 50, leave it out and
101	say why in chat if it was interesting.
102	
103	## Step 6 — build the spreadsheet
104	
105	Write the roles to JSON and run the bundled script — it owns the column layout, tier colours,
106	fit colour-scale, filters and the "Search notes" sheet, so week-to-week shortlists stay
107	comparable and no run has to reinvent openpyxl:
108	
109	```bash
110	python3 scripts/build_shortlist.py --in roles.json --out "Role shortlist — 5 Aug 2026.xlsx"
111	```
112	
113	The JSON shape is documented in the script's docstring. Fill `sweep_notes` — sources swept,
114	queries run, raw/gated/verified counts, notable drops — because that sheet is how he judges
115	whether the search covered the ground. Then deliver the file with `SendUserFile`.
116	
117	## Step 7 — report briefly in chat
118	
119	Short and useful; the spreadsheet holds the detail. Roughly:
120	
121	- One line on what was swept and what came back (`19 verified from ~60 candidates`).
122	- The top three, one line each: role, company, and the specific reason it fits.
123	- What to do first — which one or two to apply to today, and why those.
124	- One honest observation: a pattern in the market, a gap in his profile that keeps costing him, or a source that came back empty.
125	
126	Don't re-tabulate the sheet in chat, and don't pad with encouragement.
127	
128	## Judgment calls
129	
130	- **"Is this posting any good for me?"** with a single link — skip the sweep entirely. Fetch it, score it against the profile, answer in chat with the honest verdict and what to emphasise if he applies. No spreadsheet unless he asks.
131	- **A named company** — fetch its board directly (`job-boards.greenhouse.io/<company>`, or an `allowed_domains` search on the company name) instead of running a generic sweep.
132	- **A repeat run** — if an earlier shortlist exists in this session or in the project, dedupe against it and mark what's new, so he isn't re-reading last week's list. Say how many were carried over.
133	- **A thin sweep** — if verification leaves only a handful, deliver the handful and say plainly what you'd change next time (different vocabulary, wider geography, contract-only pass). Don't inflate the sheet.
134	- **He corrects a preference** — a rate expectation, a company he'd never join, a city he would move to — write it into `references/candidate-profile.md` so the next run inherits it.
135	- **Something in the sweep is worth acting on beyond applying** (a company hiring three roles he fits, a recruiter contact in the posting) — mention it in the chat reply; it's often more valuable than one more row.
136	
137	## Files in this skill
138	
139	```
140	job-hunt/
141	├── SKILL.md
142	├── references/
143	│   ├── candidate-profile.md   — what "good fit" means; keep it current
144	│   └── sources.md             — tested search playbook, dead ends, verification traps
145	└── scripts/
146	    └── build_shortlist.py     — roles JSON → formatted .xlsx shortlist
147	```

112	- **Lever:** `https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/<co>?mode=json` → `workplaceType` (Remote/Hybrid), location. Fails on very large aggregator boards.
113	- **Workable:** `https://apply.workable.com/api/v1/widget/accounts/<subdomain>?details=true` → the only readable route into Workable.

116	"list all jobs" on a big board returned 7 of N and omitted roles that exist. Ask a *targeted*
117	question instead — "does this board currently list a Forward Deployed Engineer role, and what
118	is its location and posted date?"

123	
124	Search indexes run stale across every ATS, so a posting found in search may already be gone.
125	These are the specific failure modes, and the first one is dangerous because the fetch
126	*succeeds*:
127	
128	1. **Greenhouse closed postings degrade to the board index.** Fetching a dead job URL returns the company's entire open-roles list with the target role absent, and nothing flags it. **Detection rule: if a single-posting fetch comes back describing many different jobs, the posting is closed.** Drop it.
129	2. **Personio closed postings hard-404** even while still indexed in search. Clean failure — just drop.
130	3. **Lever snippets misstate location.** Fetch the posting and read the location from the page body.
131	4. **"Remote" ≠ eligible.** Read the eligibility sentence, not the word "Remote" in the title. Titles like "AI Automation Engineer (Remote – ES/UK only)" are common, and boards sometimes label a region-locked role "worldwide".
132	5. **Aggregators masquerade as employers.** Jobgether, Jobgether-on-Lever, and similar reposts have no named end client. Skip them; find the original posting if the role looks good.
133	6. **Himalayas orders results non-chronologically** — page 1 mixed "2 mins ago" with "27 days ago". Read the date on each row rather than trusting position.

139	- Minute-level ages: euremotejobs, remoterocketship, himalayas, aijobs.net (parse from the page).
140	- Sortable by recency in the URL: only `remoterocketship.com/?sort=DateAdded` is verified.
141	- Programmatic date filtering: only via the JSON APIs (`created_at` / `date` / `epoch` / `updated_at`).
142	- No board tested exposes a verified "posted within N days" parameter — filter client-side.

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Turn a verified list of roles into a formatted .xlsx shortlist.

Usage:
    python3 scripts/build_shortlist.py --in roles.json --out "shortlist.xlsx"

Why this exists: every job sweep otherwise reinvents the same openpyxl formatting, and
inconsistent columns make two shortlists impossible to compare week to week. Write the
roles as JSON, let this handle the spreadsheet.

Input JSON:
{
  "search_label": "AI + automation, remote-eligible from Italy - 5 Aug 2026",
  "candidate": "Prabhavit Gupta",
  "sweep_notes": {
      "raw_candidates": 62, "after_gates": 28, "verified_live": 19,
      "sources_searched": ["Ashby via allowed_domains", "euremotejobs Europe region"],
      "queries": ["AI automation engineer remote Europe"],
      "dropped_examples": ["Acme AI Engineer - US-only, no contractors"]
  },
  "roles": [{
      "title": "AI Solutions Engineer", "company": "Camunda", "url": "https://...",
      "fit": 87, "track": "A - AI/Automation", "basis": "Employee",
      "location": "Remote - EMEA", "eligibility": "Tier 1",
      "comp": "EUR 65,000-80,000", "posted": "2026-07-29 (7d)",
      "why": "...", "watch_outs": "...", "source": "Ashby search",
      "verified": "fetched 2026-08-05 - live"
  }]
}

Only title, company and url are required. Everything else degrades to "-".
"""

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.formatting.rule import ColorScaleRule
from openpyxl.styles import Alignment, Border, Font, PatternFill, Side
from openpyxl.utils import get_column_letter

COLUMNS = [
    ("fit", "Fit", 6),
    ("title", "Role", 38),
    ("company", "Company", 20),
    ("track", "Track", 16),
    ("basis", "Basis", 11),
    ("location", "Location / remote", 24),
    ("eligibility", "Eligibility", 13),
    ("comp", "Comp / rate", 20),
    ("posted", "Posted", 16),
    ("why", "Why it fits", 52),
    ("watch_outs", "Watch-outs", 34),
    ("url", "Link", 14),
    ("source", "Found via", 18),
    ("verified", "Verified", 22),
]

WRAPPED = {"title", "why", "watch_outs", "location", "comp", "verified"}

HEADER_FILL = PatternFill("solid", fgColor="1F3864")
HEADER_FONT = Font(bold=True, color="FFFFFF", size=11)
TITLE_FONT = Font(bold=True, size=14, color="1F3864")
LINK_FONT = Font(color="0563C1", underline="single")
THIN = Side(style="thin", color="D9D9D9")
BORDER = Border(left=THIN, right=THIN, top=THIN, bottom=THIN)

TIER_FILLS = {
    "1": PatternFill("solid", fgColor="E2EFDA"),  # workable from Italy today
    "2": PatternFill("solid", fgColor="DDEBF7"),  # non-EU Europe, remote
    "3": PatternFill("solid", fgColor="FFF2CC"),  # relocation / sponsorship
}


def tier_key(value):
    """Pull a tier digit out of free text like 'Tier 1 - workable from Italy'."""
    for ch in str(value):
        if ch in "123":
            return ch
    return None


def clean_roles(roles):
    """Drop unusable rows, dedupe, clamp fit, sort best-first."""
    seen, out, problems = set(), [], []
    for i, r in enumerate(roles):
        missing = [f for f in ("title", "company", "url") if not str(r.get(f, "")).strip()]
        if missing:
            problems.append(f"row {i + 1}: missing {', '.join(missing)} - skipped")
            continue
        key = (r["company"].strip().lower(), r["title"].strip().lower())
        if key in seen:
            problems.append(f"duplicate dropped: {r['title']} @ {r['company']}")
            continue
        seen.add(key)
        try:
            r["fit"] = max(0, min(100, int(round(float(r.get("fit", 0))))))
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            r["fit"] = 0
            problems.append(f"{r['title']} @ {r['company']}: unreadable fit score, set to 0")
        if not str(r.get("url", "")).startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            problems.append(f"{r['title']} @ {r['company']}: link is not a URL - check it")
        out.append(r)
    out.sort(key=lambda r: (-r["fit"], r["company"].lower()))
    return out, problems


def estimate_height(role):
    """Rough row height so wrapped text isn't clipped."""
    lines = 1
    for field, width in (("why", 52), ("watch_outs", 34), ("title", 38)):
        text = str(role.get(field, ""))
        lines = max(lines, -(-len(text) // max(width - 4, 10)))
    return min(120, max(30, lines * 14))


def write_shortlist(ws, roles, label):
    ws.cell(row=1, column=1, value=label).font = TITLE_FONT

Swept Ashby, both Greenhouse hosts, join.com, SmartRecruiters, Personio and Lever for n8n/agent vocabulary, then verified live status and pay through the companies' own ATS APIs. ~55 raw candidates, 20 passed the profile gates, **5 survived verification**. Thin, and the reason is worth knowing: this niche is full of postings that are closed or not actually open to you.

**The pay picture first, since that was the question.** Three of the five publish a band, and all three are in USD or GBP — the disclosure is coming from US pay-transparency law, not from European employers getting better at it. No EUR band anywhere in the sweep.

- **Arize AI — Forward Deployed AI Engineer, EMEA — $125k–175k + equity.** Remote EMEA. The only posting here asking for **2–5 years** rather than 5+, at an AI-observability company where the product is LLM/agent tooling and the job is deploying it into customer environments. That is the FlowSpace pattern with a bigger logo.
- **Camunda — AI Forward Deployed Engineer, EMEA — $157k–254k / £99k–162k.** "Fully remote and global." Process orchestration, and the role is explicitly building AI agents into customer workflows and wiring legacy APIs — your integration record maps straight on. Java and BPMN are the catch; neither is yours.
- **OpenHands (All Hands AI) — Enterprise Agent Engineer — $170k–225k base + bonus + equity.** Agents *are* the product; Python, LLMs, MCP and Claude Code all named. Wants 5+ years against your ~3, so it's a stretch — but the 1+ year of shipping agents you clear outright.

Zapier's Applied AI role is on-theme and remote-native but hides its band and its excluded-country list, and n8n's own board has nothing in AI/agents — details in the sheet.

**Do these two today:** Arize, because the years-of-experience line finally matches and the comp is on the page; then OpenHands, as the deliberate stretch — a company whose entire product is agents will read "shipped agents in production" as the qualification and treat the year count as secondary.

**The honest observation.** n8n the company is *not* hiring for n8n work. Four postings — AI Workflow Automation Engineer, Senior Solutions Engineer (Remote Europe), Senior AI Engineer, Sr AI Engineer — all show up in search and all are absent from their live Ashby board on two separate checks. Closed, with only stale search results keeping them visible. That pattern held across the niche: the single best keyword match in the whole sweep was **NICE, "Software Engineer (AI, N8N, MCP)"** — hands-on n8n, MCP servers, AI agent patterns, only 2+ years required — and it's Pune, India, hybrid two days in office. **Cresta** wanted a Senior FDE for AI agents at $185k–235k and requires US work authorisation. The n8n/agent demand is real and the pay is real, but it is concentrated in US-payroll and India-delivery roles; your leverage is being one of the few people who can do it *and* already holds EU work rights, so lead with that rather than treating it as a footnote.

One thing to tell me, because it changes how I rank from here: **what number do you actually want?** Three of these disclose and I've been reporting the bands as published rather than judging them. Give me a floor — salary or day rate — and I'll score against it and stop surfacing roles that pay under it.

Also worth noting: every USD band above sits at a company with no stated EU entity. For those, the realistic route is a contractor engagement, which is your normal mode anyway — ask about it in the first call rather than at offer stage.

**What produced results:** Ashby via `allowed_domains` was the best source by a distance (Camunda, OpenHands, Zapier, plus the n8n leads). The Greenhouse `.com`/`.eu` pair produced Arize AI and the NICE n8n/MCP role. The Ashby posting API (`?includeCompensation=true`) was the most valuable verification tool — it settled live-status *and* pay in one call. The unrestricted contract-vocabulary query returned nothing usable: forum posts, Contra, itjobswatch, no employer postings. The Lever/join.com query returned almost entirely aggregators (3× Jobgether, Smart Working Solutions, a legal recruiter), exactly as `sources.md` predicts.

**Verified roles:** Arize AI FDE AI Engineer EMEA (84, $125–175k), Camunda AI FDE EMEA (76, $157–254k/£99–162k), OpenHands Enterprise Agent Engineer (74, $170–225k), Zapier Engineer Applied AI (69, no band), n8n Sr Growth Engineer (62, no band).

**Notable finding:** all four n8n AI/Solutions/AI-Engineer postings that surface in search are closed — absent from n8n's live Ashby board API on two independent targeted reads. The best keyword match in the whole sweep (NICE, "Software Engineer (AI, N8N, MCP)", 2+ yrs, hands-on n8n + MCP + agent patterns) is Pune hybrid. Cresta's $185–235k agent FDE requires US authorisation.

**Issues with the skill's instructions:**

1. **`sources.md` §2 oversells Ashby's individual posting pages.** Three of them (all n8n) returned unrendered JS shells — `meta-title: Jobs` and "You need to enable JavaScript". The playbook documents this failure only for `apply.workable.com` and calls Ashby the "best single source" with a "clean parse". Four other Ashby fetches in the same batch rendered fine, so it's intermittent, but it cost me 3 wasted calls and nearly cost me the highest-relevance company in the sweep. Worth adding: *if an Ashby posting page returns a JS shell, fall back to the org's posting API.*

2. **The §5 truncation warning is right but undersells the danger.** My first n8n board-API call didn't just under-report — it returned 2 jobs and affirmatively stated the four target titles were "not present". That's a fabricated negative, not an omission. Even the second, narrowly-targeted call returned only one job. I only trusted the "closed" conclusion because two independent reads agreed. The guidance should say plainly that a *negative* answer from a truncated board-API fetch is not evidence until confirmed twice.

3. **Step 4's Greenhouse "many jobs = closed" detection rule has no Ashby equivalent**, which is the gap that made (1) and (2) hard — a JS shell and a truncated API both look like "role absent" and neither is self-evidently a fetch failure.

4. **Minor:** Step 6's example command uses a relative `scripts/` path; from the mandated output directory I had to use an absolute path. And `roles.json`'s documented schema has no field for "peer comp at the same company" — relevant on a pay-focused sweep — so I put it in a non-schema key that the script silently ignores.

One judgment call flagged for you: the n8n Sr Growth Engineer is 77 days old, past the 30-day freshness frame, but confirmed `isListed=true` via the ATS API. I included it at 62 with the staleness flagged, on the grounds that confirmed-live beats posting age.
